### TH-001: Motor Thermal Overload
**Equipment Type:** Motor  
**Symptoms:** Temperature reading exceeds max_temp_c by 5-15°C; persistent over 10+ minutes.  
**Root Causes:** Bearing friction increase (worn bearings), misalignment, cooling system failure, sustained overload.  
**Detection Method:** Infrared thermal camera; correlate with vibration (if vibration also high, bearings likely failing).  
**Recommended Action:** 
1. Reduce load immediately if possible
2. Inspect bearing for heat, grinding sounds
3. Check cooling system (air intake, fan operation)
4. If persistent after cooling restart, schedule bearing replacement

**Parts to Stage:** Bearing replacement kit (6208 or 6309 per equipment), lubricant (ISO 32 turbine oil), thermal paste.  
**Typical Lead Time:** 2-3 days (bearings); 1 day (lubricant).

### TH-002: Pump Seal Thermal Spike
**Equipment Type:** Pump  
**Symptoms:** Temperature spike 10-20°C above baseline, localized at pump housing seal area.  
**Root Causes:** Seal degradation, friction from contaminated fluid, misalignment.  
**Detection Method:** Dual IR cameras (one on motor, one on pump body); note if motor is cool but pump hot (seal-specific issue).  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Check pump discharge pressure (high pressure + hot seal = friction issue)
2. Monitor for fluid leaks (indicates seal failure imminent)
3. If leak detected, schedule immediate seal replacement
4. If no leak, increase inspection frequency to daily

**Parts to Stage:** Pump seal assembly (SA-42 for standard pumps), hydraulic fluid (ISO 46 per spec).  
**Typical Lead Time:** 3-5 days (seal assembly); 2 days (fluid).

### TH-003: Compressor Piston Ring Thermal Anomaly
**Equipment Type:** Compressor  
**Symptoms:** Sustained high discharge temperature (90-100°C) even after cooldown; motor current draw increases 10-15%.  
**Root Causes:** Worn piston rings (blow-by), valve leakage, inadequate lubrication.  
**Detection Method:** Temperature sensor on discharge line; cross-check with motor current (ammeter).  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Reduce compression ratio if possible (unload compressor)
2. Inspect oil level; top off if low
3. Listen for grinding or metallic sounds (piston ring damage)
4. If motor current remains elevated after oil top-off, schedule ring replacement

**Parts to Stage:** Piston ring kit (PR-88), compressor oil (mineral, ISO 46).  
**Typical Lead Time:** 5-7 days (ring kit, requires internal inspection); 1 day (oil).

---

### VB-001: Motor Bearing Wear Signature
**Equipment Type:** Motor  
**Symptoms:** Vibration amplitude 1.5-2x baseline (baseline typically 1-2 mm/s); localized at bearing housings.  
**Root Causes:** Bearing wear, misalignment, unbalance.  
**Detection Method:** Accelerometer on bearing housing; spectrum analysis (look for 1x, 2x, 3x running speed peaks and bearing defect frequencies).  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Measure runout at bearing housing (if >0.5mm, likely misalignment or wear)
2. If vibration worsens over hours, schedule immediate bearing replacement
3. If stable, increase monitoring to every 4 hours until replacement scheduled

**Parts to Stage:** Replacement bearing (match equipment_id in database), alignment shims, bearing puller tool.  
**Typical Lead Time:** 2-3 days (bearing); tools on-site.

### VB-002: Pump Cavitation Signature
**Equipment Type:** Pump  
**Symptoms:** Broadband high-frequency noise (>10 kHz) and vibration; erratic displacement.  
**Root Causes:** Inlet pressure too low, suction line blockage, fluid viscosity too high.  
**Detection Method:** Accelerometer on pump inlet; spectrum shows high-frequency rumble; audible grinding.  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Check inlet strainer (likely blocked); replace strainer element
2. Verify inlet pressure gauge (should be >0.3 bar gauge; below 0 = cavitation imminent)
3. If strainer clear and pressure low, check suction line for kinks/blockages
4. If cavitation persists, reduce flow demand (throttle outlet pressure)

**Parts to Stage:** Pump inlet strainer element, hose clamps, suction line check valve (if worn).  
**Typical Lead Time:** 1 day (strainer element, on-site); 2 days (check valve if replacement needed).

### VB-003: Fan Blade Imbalance
**Equipment Type:** Fan  
**Symptoms:** Vibration 2-3x baseline, fundamental frequency = running speed (1x), directional (may only appear on specific axis).  
**Root Causes:** Blade fouling (dust/dirt accumulation), blade crack, bearing wear.  
**Detection Method:** Accelerometer on fan bearing housing, measure on multiple planes (radial, axial).  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Visually inspect fan blades for dirt, cracks, deformation
2. Clean blades and shroud if fouled (especially in humid plants)
3. If vibration still high after cleaning, suspect bearing wear (see VB-001)
4. If blade visibly cracked, schedule immediate replacement

**Parts to Stage:** Replacement fan blade set, bearing replacement kit, cleaning supplies.  
**Typical Lead Time:** 2-3 days (blades); 2-3 days (bearings).

---

### AC-001: Air Leak (High-Frequency Whistle)
**Equipment Type:** Compressor, Pump (pressurized systems)  
**Symptoms:** High-frequency hissing/whistling sound; ultrasonic microphone detects 20-40 kHz spikes; audible in quiet environment.  
**Root Causes:** Gasket failure, threaded connection loosened, seal degradation, pressure relief valve stuck open.  
**Detection Method:** Ultrasonic microphone array (pinpoint leak location by triangulation); acoustic frequency analysis.  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Locate leak using ultrasonic probe (triangulate if possible)
2. If leak at connection, tighten gently (do not over-torque)
3. If leak at gasket, depressurize and replace gasket
4. If leak at relief valve, clean or replace valve cartridge
5. Monitor pressure downstream (if dropping, leak confirmed and significant)

**Parts to Stage:** Gasket kit (fluid-specific: air, hydraulic, refrigerant), thread sealant (PTFE tape), relief valve cartridge.  
**Typical Lead Time:** 1-2 days (gaskets, cartridges, tape on-site).

### AC-002: Motor Grinding Noise (Bearing Damage)
**Equipment Type:** Motor  
**Symptoms:** Grinding, scraping, or irregular metallic rattle; worsens under load; distinct from normal hum.  
**Root Causes:** Bearing race failure, loose rotor bar, internal short circuit.  
**Detection Method:** Acoustic monitoring (low-frequency rumble typically indicates bearing failure); correlate with temperature (if temp normal but grinding present, may be electrical short).  
**Recommended Action:**
1. Shut down immediately (bearing failure is imminent)
2. Inspect bearing housing for heat, smells (burned insulation = electrical issue)
3. Do not restart under load until inspected
4. Schedule bearing replacement or motor rewind (if electrical)

**Parts to Stage:** Replacement bearing, motor rewind service (if needed), lubricant.  
**Typical Lead Time:** 2-3 days (bearing); 5-7 days (motor rewind service).

MOTOR THERMAL OVERLOAD RESPONSE (MP-TH-001)
MAINTENANCE PLAYBOOK: MOTOR THERMAL OVERLOAD RESPONSE
Equipment Type: Motor (all models 6208, 6309 bearings)
Procedure ID: MP-TH-001
Last Updated: 2026-09-01
Authority: Regional Engineering Team

OVERVIEW
--------
This playbook covers response to motor thermal overload alerts (temperature exceeding max_temp_c by 5+ degrees Celsius). The procedure prioritizes immediate safety and minimizes equipment downtime through systematic diagnosis.

SEVERITY LEVELS
---------------
Level 1 (Yellow): Temperature 2-5°C above max; stable for <5 minutes → Increase monitoring
Level 2 (Orange): Temperature 5-10°C above max; sustained >5 minutes → Reduce load and diagnose
Level 3 (Red): Temperature 10°C+ above max; rising → Shut down immediately

STEP 1: IMMEDIATE RESPONSE (First 5 minutes)
---------------------------------------------
Action 1.1: Acknowledge Alert
- Log alert timestamp and equipment_id in maintenance system
- Note current load/duty cycle (full load, part load, idle)

Action 1.2: Assess Severity
- Read current temperature from sensor
- Compare to baseline (check equipment.csv for max_temp_c)
- If temperature exceeding max + 10°C and rising, proceed to Step 2
- If temperature stable or slowly dropping, proceed to Step 3

Action 1.3: Safety Check
- Verify motor is accessible (no personnel in pinch points)
- Check for visible smoke, burning smell, or fluid leaks
- If any danger signs, shut down immediately and clear area

STEP 2: EMERGENCY SHUTDOWN (if temp >max + 10°C)
--------------------------------------------------
Action 2.1: Load Reduction
- If possible, reduce motor load by 50% immediately
- Do NOT abruptly stop motor (thermal shock can damage windings)
- Allow 2-3 minute coast-down if equipment allows

Action 2.2: Shutdown
- Turn off motor starter using main control panel
- Allow motor to cool naturally for 15 minutes (do not force cool with water/air)

MOTOR THERMAL OVERLOAD RESPONSE (MP-TH-001)
Action 2.3: Escalate
- Contact shift supervisor immediately
- Flag equipment_id for urgent inspection (same day)
- Do not restart without supervisor and engineering approval

STEP 3: SYSTEMATIC DIAGNOSIS (temp 5-10°C above max, stable)
--------------------------------------------------------------
Action 3.1: Check Cooling System
- Visually inspect air intake to motor for blockage (dirt, debris)
- Verify cooling fan running (listen for hum; check for blade rotation)
- Check for kinks in cooling hose/ductwork
- Clean air intake if clogged (use compressed air, never water on running motor)
- Allow 5 minutes for temperature recovery

If temperature normalizes after cooling inspection:
→ Go to Step 5: Post-Incident Monitoring

If temperature remains elevated:
→ Continue to Action 3.2

Action 3.2: Check Bearing/Mechanical Load
- Stop motor (coast-down if equipment allows)
- Feel bearing housings by hand (use thermal glove if concerned)
  - Normal: warm but can hold hand for 3+ seconds
  - Abnormal: too hot to touch for more than 1 second
- Listen for grinding, squealing, or rough sounds (bearing wear indicator)
- If bearing feels excessively hot or sounds rough:
  → Go to Action 3.3 (Bearing Replacement Needed)
  → Schedule ASAP; Stage parts (see Parts List section)

If bearing feels normal but mechanical load seems high:
→ Check motor alignment (use dial indicator if available, <0.05mm runout acceptable)
→ If misaligned, note for corrective action; escalate to maintenance planner

Action 3.3: Check Electrical Load (if bearing normal, cooling normal)
- Contact plant electrician
- Verify motor current draw with clamp ammeter
  - Normal: <1.2x nameplate current
  - Abnormal: >1.2x nameplate current = possible winding short or high load from driven equipment
- If current high and mechanical load normal: likely electrical fault in motor or upstream
  → Escalate to electrical maintenance; do not restart until cleared

MOTOR THERMAL OVERLOAD RESPONSE (MP-TH-001)
STEP 4: BEARING REPLACEMENT (if bearing wear confirmed)
---------------------------------------------------------
Action 4.1: Prepare
- Schedule replacement during next available maintenance window
- Verify parts availability (see Parts List section; typical lead time 2-3 days)
- Alert operations of planned downtime
- Request bearing puller tool and alignment kit from tool crib

Action 4.2: Bearing Removal & Installation
- Disconnect motor from power (lockout/tagout procedure)
- Locate bearing designation on bearing housing (should match equipment.csv bearing_type)
- Use bearing puller to remove old bearing (do not tap directly; use puller to avoid race damage)
- Clean bearing journal with lint-free cloth
- Pack new bearing with appropriate grease (see Parts List: Lubricant Type)
- Install new bearing using bearing installer tool (press slowly, support inner race only)
- Spin bearing by hand to ensure free rotation (no grinding)

Action 4.3: Verify & Restart
- Reconnect motor to power
- Run at 50% load for 10 minutes; monitor temperature (should stabilize within 5°C of baseline)
- Check for unusual sounds or vibration
- If temperature and noise normal, return to full load
- Document bearing replacement in maintenance log with date, bearing part number, and technician name

STEP 5: POST-INCIDENT MONITORING
----------------------------------
Action 5.1: Short-term (24-48 hours)
- Increase monitoring frequency to every 2 hours
- Log temperature and load at each check
- If temperature exceeds baseline + 3°C at any point: repeat diagnosis from Step 3

Action 5.2: Medium-term (1-4 weeks)
- Reduce monitoring to every 8 hours
- Continue daily logs
- Compare trending: if temperature creeping upward despite normal load, bearing replacement likely needed soon

MOTOR THERMAL OVERLOAD RESPONSE (MP-TH-001)
Action 5.3: Root Cause Documentation
- Complete incident summary: what was root cause (cooling system, bearing wear, electrical)?
- Note any preventive measures taken
- Share findings with shift team (whiteboard briefing or email)

PARTS LIST: MOTOR THERMAL OVERLOAD

Part Name                    | Part Number | Supplier  | Lead Time | Cost
Bearing 6208 (Ball)         | 6208-2RS    | Supplier-A | 2 days    | $45
Bearing 6309 (Ball)         | 6309-2RS    | Supplier-A | 2 days    | $60
Lubricant (ISO 32 turbine)  | OIL-ISO32   | Supplier-A | 1 day     | $25
Thermal Paste (motor mfg)   | THERM-MP01  | Supplier-B | 1 day     | $12
Bearing Puller Kit          | TOOL-BP10   | On-site   | N/A       | N/A (tool crib)

EQUIPMENT MAPPING
Equipment-001, Equipment-002, Equipment-009, Equipment-012, Equipment-016, Equipment-018:
→ Use Bearing 6208-2RS

Equipment-006, Equipment-011, Equipment-015, Equipment-020:
→ Use Bearing 6309-2RS

All motors: Use OIL-ISO32 and THERM-MP01

PUMP SEAL REPLACEMENT (MP-SEAL-001)
MAINTENANCE PLAYBOOK: PUMP SEAL REPLACEMENT
Equipment Type: Pump (seal-type SA-42)
Procedure ID: MP-SEAL-001
Last Updated: 2026-08-28
Authority: Regional Engineering Team

OVERVIEW
--------
Pump seals (SA-42) are critical to preventing fluid leakage and maintaining system pressure. This playbook covers replacement when thermal spikes or visible leaks indicate seal failure.

DIAGNOSIS: SEAL FAILURE INDICATORS
-----------------------------------
- Visible fluid weeping from pump housing (droplets within 5 minutes of shutdown)
- Thermal spike at seal area (TH-002 anomaly signature)
- Increased noise or vibration at pump inlet
- Sustained pressure drop in system

STEP 1: ASSESS & PREPARE
------------------------
- Verify equipment_id and pump type (should match equipment.csv)
- Shut down pump and depressurize system (open relief valve or bleed screw)
- Place collection tray under seal area to catch residual fluid
- Allow 15 minutes for pressure to bleed off and fluid to drain

STEP 2: SEAL REMOVAL
--------------------
- Disconnect pump from motor (uncouple)
- Remove pump from service line (unbolt from manifold)
- Place pump on bench in clean area
- Locate seal cartridge (visible as cylindrical component at pump output)
- Using seal puller tool, carefully extract old seal (do not damage bore)
- Clean bore thoroughly with lint-free cloth; inspect for scoring or corrosion
  - Light scoring acceptable (can seal against); deep score requires bore honing or seal replacement
- Rinse bore with compatible fluid (ISO 46 hydraulic oil) to remove debris

STEP 3: SEAL INSTALLATION
--------------------------
- Install new seal cartridge (SA-42) into bore
- Use seal installer tool to seat seal evenly (no forcing)
- Spin pump shaft by hand to ensure seal does not bind (should spin freely)
- Fill pump cavity with hydraulic fluid (ISO 46) to prime pump

PUMP SEAL REPLACEMENT (MP-SEAL-001)
STEP 4: REASSEMBLY & TESTING
-----------------------------
- Couple pump back to motor
- Reinstall pump in service line (bolt to manifold)
- Pressurize system slowly (open relief valve to limit pressure to 50% of max for first 5 minutes)
- Monitor seal area for leaks (none acceptable; even droplets indicate misalignment)
- If leak-free for 5 minutes, increase pressure to 75%, monitor another 5 minutes
- If still leak-free, run at full operating pressure and monitor temperature
  - Seal should stabilize at baseline temperature within 15 minutes
  - If temperature spikes, shut down and re-seat seal (misalignment)

STEP 5: SIGN-OFF
----------------
- Document seal replacement: date, pump equipment_id, old/new part numbers, technician name
- Return old seal for analysis (helps identify why it failed: cavitation, dry-run, contamination)
- Schedule follow-up inspection in 24-48 hours

PARTS LIST
-----------
Seal Assembly SA-42      | SEAL-SA42   | Supplier-C | 3-5 days | $180
Hydraulic Fluid ISO 46   | OIL-ISO46   | Supplier-C | 2 days   | $50
Seal Puller/Installer Kit| TOOL-SEAL   | On-site   | N/A      | N/A

COMPRESSOR PISTON RING MAINTENANCE (MP-COMP-001)
MAINTENANCE PLAYBOOK: COMPRESSOR PISTON RING MAINTENANCE
Equipment Type: Compressor
Procedure ID: MP-COMP-001
Last Updated: 2026-09-05
Authority: Regional Engineering Team

[Abbreviated version for brevity; would include similar steps as above but focused on ring replacement, oil top-off procedures, and compression testing]

OVERVIEW: Piston ring wear reduces compression efficiency, increases discharge temperature, and raises motor current. Early detection and replacement prevents catastrophic failure.

DIAGNOSTICS
- High discharge temperature (90-100°C baseline)
- Elevated motor current (>1.2x normal)
- Oil consumption rate increasing (top-offs more frequent than normal)

BASIC RESPONSE
1. Check oil level; top off if low (use compressor oil PR-88)
2. Monitor discharge temperature for 24 hours
3. If temperature does not drop within 5°C after oil top-off: schedule ring replacement (5-7 day lead time)

PARTS LIST
Piston Ring Kit PR-88    | RING-PR88   | Supplier-B | 5-7 days | $320
Compressor Oil ISO 46    | OIL-COMP46  | Supplier-B | 1 day    | $65

BEARING VIBRATION DIAGNOSIS & REPLACEMENT (MP-VB-BEARING)
MAINTENANCE PLAYBOOK: BEARING VIBRATION DIAGNOSIS & REPLACEMENT
Equipment Type: Motor, Fan, Pump (all equipment with rolling element bearings)
Procedure ID: MP-VB-BEARING
Last Updated: 2026-08-30
Authority: Regional Engineering Team

OVERVIEW
--------
Vibration anomalies often indicate bearing wear or misalignment. This playbook covers systematic diagnosis to distinguish bearing failure from other mechanical issues.

STEP 1: MEASURE VIBRATION
--------------------------
- Place accelerometer on bearing housing (typically on top)
- Measure peak vibration in mm/s (compare to baseline in equipment.csv column max_vibration_mm_s)
- If vibration <1.2x baseline: normal (return to routine monitoring)
- If vibration 1.2-1.5x baseline: elevated but not critical; increase inspection frequency to every 4 hours
- If vibration >1.5x baseline: urgent (bearing wear suspected); proceed to Action 1.2

STEP 2: ANALYZE VIBRATION SPECTRUM (if equipment >1.2x baseline)
-----------------------------------------------------------------
- If vibration is broadband (uniform across frequencies 0-10 kHz): likely bearing race defect or misalignment
- If vibration shows discrete peaks at running speed and harmonics (1x, 2x, 3x): likely unbalance
- If vibration shows random spikes: cavitation (for pumps) or loose rotor bars (for motors)

STEP 3: CORRECTIVE ACTIONS
---------------------------

IF BEARING WEAR SUSPECTED (broadband vibration, feels hot):
→ Replace bearing (see BEARING REPLACEMENT procedure, MP-TH-001 Step 4)

IF UNBALANCE SUSPECTED (1x, 2x peaks):
→ For motors/fans: clean blades or check for missing weights; balance if needed
→ For pumps: inspect impeller for damage; replace if cracked

IF MISALIGNMENT SUSPECTED (broadband, but bearing not hot):
→ Measure runout between shafts (should be <0.05mm)
→ If misaligned: re-align and repeat vibration measurement
→ If vibration improves >20%, misalignment confirmed and corrected

BEARING VIBRATION DIAGNOSIS & REPLACEMENT (MP-VB-BEARING)
IF CAVITATION (pump vibration + broadband noise + pressure drop):
→ Follow MP-PUMP-CAVITATION playbook (clean inlet strainer, verify inlet pressure)

PARTS: Standard bearing kit (see MP-TH-001 for specific bearings)

Part BEARING-6208-2RS: Ball Bearing 6208-2RS (20mm ID, 47mm OD, 14mm width). For Motor. Compatible: Equipment-001, Equipment-002, Equipment-009, Equipment-012, Equipment-016, Equipment-018. Supplier Supplier-A, $45, lead time 2 days. Standard motor bearing. Keep 3 units in stock.

Part BEARING-6309-2RS: Ball Bearing 6309-2RS (45mm ID, 100mm OD, 25mm width). For Motor, Fan. Compatible: Equipment-006, Equipment-011, Equipment-015, Equipment-020. Supplier Supplier-A, $60, lead time 2 days. Larger motor/fan bearing. Keep 2 units in stock.

Part SEAL-SA42: Pump Seal Assembly SA-42 (for standard hydraulic pumps). For Pump. Compatible: Equipment-004, Equipment-008, Equipment-013, Equipment-017. Supplier Supplier-C, $180, lead time 5 days. Critical component; 5-day lead time is typical. Recommend pre-staging when thermal spike detected.

Part RING-PR88: Piston Ring Kit PR-88 (for reciprocating compressors). For Compressor. Compatible: Equipment-005, Equipment-010, Equipment-014, Equipment-019. Supplier Supplier-B, $320, lead time 6 days. Long lead time (6-7 days). Requires internal inspection; not a quick field replacement.

Part OIL-ISO32: Turbine Oil ISO 32 (for electric motor cooling and bearing lubrication). For Motor. Compatible: . Supplier Supplier-A, $25, lead time 1 days. Stock item; usually available next day. Use for motor bearing lubrication and thermal management.

Part OIL-ISO46: Hydraulic Fluid ISO 46 (for pumps and hydraulic systems). For Pump, Compressor. Compatible: . Supplier Supplier-C, $50, lead time 2 days. Standard pump fluid; 2-day lead time. Verify compatibility with pump manufacturer before use.

Part OIL-COMP46: Compressor Oil ISO 46 (mineral-based, for piston/screw compressors). For Compressor. Compatible: . Supplier Supplier-B, $65, lead time 1 days. Mineral oil; do not mix with synthetic. Essential for piston ring lubrication.

Part THERM-MP01: Thermal Paste (motor-grade, for bearing/housing thermal interface). For Motor. Compatible: . Supplier Supplier-B, $12, lead time 1 days. Used for bearing housing thermal monitoring (IR sensor contact). Stock item.

Part STRAINER-PUMP: Pump Inlet Strainer Element (replacement, for cavitation prevention). For Pump. Compatible: . Supplier Supplier-C, $35, lead time 1 days. Consumable; replace annually or when VB-002 (cavitation) symptoms appear.

Part CHECK-VALVE-SUCTION: Suction Line Check Valve (prevents backflow, for pump inlet). For Pump. Compatible: . Supplier Supplier-C, $85, lead time 2 days. Used when inlet pressure consistently below 0.3 bar. Standard replacement for cavitation fix.
Scheduled cleaning for Equipment-001: every Monday at 06:00, method wet-wash, duration 2 hours. Expected effects: humidity elevation 20, temp drop 5.
Scheduled maintenance for Equipment-005: every Thursday at 14:00, method bearing_replacement, duration 2 hours. Expected effects: vibration spike 8.
Environmental baseline for Equipment-001 (post cleaning): location Floor-1-North, humidity baseline 50, humidity max expected 75, humidity elevated for hours 2.
Environmental baseline for Equipment-005 (summer season): temperature baseline 28, temperature max expected 32.
